newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebel spokesman says demands negotiable.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebel spokesman says demands negotiable.

text.p: Peruvian Marxist rebels holding hostage 83 people at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima are prepared to negotiate their demands for the release of 400 jailed colleagues and could settle for an "intermediate solution", the rebel representative in Europe said on Sunday.

"We still insist on the liberation of the political prisoners, but we consider that an intermediate solution can be reached," Isaac Velazco, European representative of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), told Reuters in a telephone interview from a European country.
It was the clearest statement yet from a rebel representative that negotiations may yet end the crisis without bloodshed.
"These are points to be debated," he said, adding that the rebels were prepared to seek "intermediate points that satisfy both sides".
Asked what that meant, he said: "Not necessarily the liberation of all the political prisoners."
He declined to give any further details of the rebel negotiating position and did not say what other components a political solution to the stand-off might entail.

But he said the release of 20 hostages on Saturday by the rebels was a gesture of flexibility in response to a first face-to-face meeting earlier in the day between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini in the ambassador's residence.

The rebels also released a statement on Saturday with one of the released hostages in which they struck a softer tone than earlier in the hostage stand-off, which began on Dec. 17 with a spectacular guerrilla raid on the diplomatic compound during a reception in honour of Japanese Emperor Akihito.

"What should be understood is that the language corresponds to the circumstances," Velazco said, adding that while the government of President Alberto Fujimori was taking a hard line by refusing to consider the rebel demands, "one is not going to be playing nice".
The three hour and 15 minute visit by Palermo to the residence on Saturday, on the other hand, was "an important step toward the political solution of this crisis", Velazco said.
The rebels had initially threatened to kill their hostages if their colleagues were not freed. As of Sunday they had released more than 420 of the original captives taken.

The area around the ambassador's residence was quiet in the early hours of Sunday as the remaining 83 hostages and about 20 rebels spent their 12th night under siege. Heavily armed police continued to cordon off an area of two city blocks on each side of the building.

Palermo, Fujimori's education minister, said following the release of the 20 hostages -- mostly Peruvian diplomats and Japanese businessmen -- that there had been "advances for the solution of this serious incident", but gave no details.
Palermo stopped short of giving the full imprimatur of the State to his talk with Cerpa, saying their conversation was "oficioso" -- a Spanish term which can mean unofficial or semi-official.
But the meeting was still a virtually unheard-of gesture from the Fujimori administration.

Fujimori himself has spoken in jail to Abimael Guzman, the captured head of the separate Shining Path rebel movement, but no official of his government has been known to speak to guerrilla leaders actively involved in hostilities.
Still being held in the residence on Sunday were Fujimori's brother, Pedro, and several high-ranking Peruvian police and government officials, as well as about 20 Japanese nationals.

A police source told Reuters that three experts from the United States were in Lima helping Peruvian police analyse conversations taking place inside the residence, which were being picked up by surveillance teams using sophisticated electronic eavesdropping devices.
The source, who declined to be named, also said other U.S. experts were advising Peruvian troops preparing for a possible last-resort assault on the compound.

Since winning elections in 1990, Fujimori, who is of Japanese origin, had cracked down on both the Shining Path and MRTA, sending troops to pursue them into remote jungle and mountain strongholds and capturing hundreds.

Until the hostage crisis he had claimed to have restored peace and order to Peru after years of guerrilla raids and bomb attacks. Japan has been the biggest donor of development aid to Peru since Fujimori came to power.
